```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(PGViS)
```

This step covers stages 1 through 6: merging replicate BAMs, calling germline
variants, joint-genotyping the cohort, converting to BED with carrier lists,
and intersecting with regulatory regions and dbSNP. It ends with an annotated
variant table loaded back into R.

None of this runs inside a vignette — it needs GATK, bedtools, a reference
genome and, realistically, a scheduler. So the shell chunks below are marked
`eval = FALSE`. The one thing we *can* do here is show the outputs each stage
produces, so you know what "done" looks like.

## The stages

```{r stages}
pgvis_stages()[, c("stage", "description")]
```

Each is a shell template with no site-specific paths in its body. When you
call the R wrapper, PGViS renders the template with a configuration block
prepended — your paths, thread count and, on SLURM, the `#SBATCH` directives.
You get a plain, readable, executable script.

Why this design rather than calling the tools from R directly: variant calling
belongs on a scheduler with tens of gigabytes of RAM per job, and you want to
be able to read, edit and resubmit the exact script that ran. Wrapping GATK in
R would hide the one artefact you most need to inspect.

## Configuration for the shell side

```{r config, eval = FALSE}
cfg <- pgvis_config(
  root            = "/scratch/me/lung_pgvis",
  reference_fasta = "/refs/hg38.analysisSet.fa",
  dbsnp_dir       = "/refs/dbsnp155/by_chr",
  regions   = list(acceptor = "/refs/acceptor.bed",
                   donor    = "/refs/donor.bed"),
  tfbs_dir  = "/refs/encode_tfbs",          # one subdirectory per TF
  cohorts   = c("luad", "lusc"),
  threads   = 8,
  scheduler = "slurm",
  slurm     = list(partition = "cpu", mem = "48G", time = "2-00:00:00",
                   cpus_per_task = 8, account = "mylab")
)
pgvis_init(cfg)
```

## The sample sheet

Three columns: cohort, tissue, sample. Validate it before you queue a thousand
jobs behind it — the check catches the failure modes that otherwise surface
hours in.

```{r sheet}
sheet <- data.frame(
  cohort = c("luad", "luad", "lusc"),
  tissue = c("blood", "solid", "blood"),
  sample = c("PT-001", "PT-001", "PT-002")
)
pgvis_sample_sheet(sheet)
```

The GVCF path is built from cohort/tissue/sample, so a duplicated triple would
have two samples overwriting each other — that is an error, not a warning. A
literal tab inside a field would shift every downstream column, so that is
caught too. With `bam_dir` supplied it also warns about samples that have no
BAM.

## Running the stages

```{r run, eval = FALSE}
pgvis_merge_bams(cfg, "samples.tsv", submit = TRUE)   # 01: merge replicates
pgvis_call_gvcf(cfg,  "samples.tsv", submit = TRUE)   # 02: HaplotypeCaller, array over chr
pgvis_combine_gvcf(cfg,    submit = TRUE)             # 03: GenomicsDBImport, array over cohort x chr
pgvis_genotype_filter(cfg, submit = TRUE)             # 04: genotype, hard-filter, normalise
pgvis_vcf_to_bed(cfg,      submit = TRUE)             # 05: BED + carriers
pgvis_intersect(cfg,       submit = TRUE)             # 06: intersect regions, then dbSNP
```

Leave `submit = FALSE` (the default) and the wrapper writes the script and
stops, so you can read it first:

```{r inspect, eval = FALSE}
script <- pgvis_call_gvcf(cfg, "samples.tsv")
cat(readLines(script), sep = "\n")
```

Any extra named argument becomes a shell variable, which is how you override a
default without touching the template:

```{r override, eval = FALSE}
pgvis_genotype_filter(
  cfg, submit = TRUE,
  FILTER_EXPR = "QD < 2.0 || FS > 60.0 || MQ < 40.0",
  JAVA_MEM    = "32g"
)
```

## Restartability is built in, not bolted on

Every stage skips outputs that already exist and are non-empty, and writes to
a temporary file that is moved into place only on success. A job killed by
walltime leaves no truncated output, and resubmitting the identical command
picks up exactly where it stopped — so there's no separate "rerun the failed
ones" step to manage. The skip check is the retry. To force a redo:

```{r force, eval = FALSE}
pgvis_intersect(cfg, submit = TRUE, PGVIS_FORCE = 1)
```

## What stage 5 produces

A headerless BED, one row per ALT allele, with allele counts and the list of
carrying samples:

```
chr1  1000  1001  A  G   1  snv  2  0.333  6  2  S1,S3
chr1  2000  2002  CT C   1  del  1  0.167  6  1  S1
chr1  2000  2002  CT CTT 2  ins  2  0.333  6  2  S2,S3
```

The carrier list and the genotype columns come from a single `awk` pass over
the VCF, so the sample order can never drift out of sync with the genotypes.
The column layout is the `"cohort"` block of the schema:

```{r schema}
pgvis_schema("splice", with_dbsnp = TRUE)[1:12]
```

If you ever edit the awk emitter, edit the schema in the same commit — they
are two halves of one contract.

## Loading it back into R

Stage 6 writes `06_dbsnp/<feature>/<cohort>_chr<N>_dbsnp.bed`.
`pgvis_load_variants()` reads all of them, applies the schema, splits
multi-allelic dbSNP records, resolves the population frequency, and builds the
coordinate keys — everything needed to turn raw intersection output into one
tidy, analysis-ready table.

```{r load, eval = FALSE}
variants <- pgvis_load_variants(cfg)
pgvis_summarise_by(variants, by = c("cohort", "feature_type"))
```

To see the shape of that table without a cluster, the package ships a
synthetic version:

```{r fixture}
variants <- pgvis_example("variants")
str(variants[, c("feature", "site_chr", "var_start", "ref", "alt",
                 "af_alt", "n_carrier", "func_site", "var_site")])
```

## What can go wrong

- **Column-count mismatch on load.** `pgvis_read_intersect()` checks the
  number of columns against the schema and stops if they disagree, rather than
  silently mislabelling. The usual cause is a region BED with an unexpected
  number of fields, or an awk emitter that was changed without the schema.
- **Empty intersections.** A feature that overlaps no variants writes an empty
  output; that is normal for rare TFs. A *majority* of features coming back
  empty usually means the region BEDs and the variants are on different genome
  builds.
- **Chromosome naming.** The variant BEDs, region BEDs and dbSNP files must all
  agree on `chr`-prefixed names. UCSC uses `chr1`; Ensembl uses `1`.
